{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"Courts are steadily moving public records onto digital systems (dockets, filings, and orders), often with the advertised goal of making justice easier to observe. That goal is laudable. But access isn't truly public when ordinary people must buy an expensive private database subscription to find and read the work of a public court. Digitization should widen the courthouse door—it shouldn't replace the steps with a tollbooth.

Private vendors can offer useful tools (bulk search, alerts, analytics), and lawyers with demanding caseloads may reasonably pay for them. The problem begins when convenience becomes necessity. A vendor's polished index doesn't create the underlying record; courts, litigants, witnesses, jurors, and taxpayers create the system that produces it. If the only usable path runs through a commercial gatekeeper, public access depends on a company's prices, contracts, and product decisions. That arrangement also narrows who can notice patterns across cases (delay, unequal treatment, recurring errors) before those patterns become impossible to ignore. That isn't a public archive. It is a private map to public law.

Supporters of paid access often point to real costs (servers, redaction, security, staff). Those costs do not disappear because a record is viewed online, and privacy concerns deserve serious treatment. Yet charging high search or retrieval fees doesn't solve privacy. It merely sorts users by ability to pay. Wealthy firms can monitor cases at scale; reporters, researchers, small practices, families, and self-represented litigants can't. Paywalls also distort which disputes receive attention, because a story, study, or community inquiry may never begin when the first search demands money and the next courthouse demands another separate payment up front. A fee wall is a dragnet turned backward—it catches people by income rather than protecting sensitive information.

Consider the practical claim that records are “available” because anyone may request them (during office hours, under local procedures). Available how? If you had to visit several clerks, learn incompatible search rules, and pay repeatedly to trace one dispute, the legal right would remain while its practical value collapsed. Digital access can reproduce that maze (one court, one portal, one fee at a time) or replace it with a coherent public system. A right that works chiefly for specialists won't serve public oversight.

Courts also shouldn't outsource accountability for design choices. Search defaults, document labels, accessibility features (including screen-reader support), and correction processes shape what the public can discover. When those choices sit behind proprietary systems, agencies may blame vendors and vendors may point back to contracts—a loop with no clear owner. We believe courts must retain responsibility for the public interface, even when private companies supply software (hosting, indexing, or maintenance).

A sound policy can protect both access and privacy. Courts should publish records through searchable, accessible portals (with no charge for ordinary use), while applying clear redaction rules to sensitive fields (such as account numbers or minors' identifying details). Bulk access may require safeguards against abuse, but those safeguards should track conduct and risk; they should not make price the proxy for trust. Contractors can still compete to sell advanced services—public infrastructure often supports valuable private tools—without becoming the only practical route to the source material. Public access should be the floor on which better tools are built, not a stripped-down demo designed to push users toward a paid tier.

Lawmakers and court administrators should set a simple baseline: public records must be meaningfully reachable by the public. That means stable portals, understandable search, accessible formats, transparent redaction standards, and fees limited to exceptional costs rather than routine viewing. It also means preserving non-digital assistance (for people without reliable devices or connections). We urge legislatures and court systems to fund that baseline directly, audit vendors openly, and require contracts that preserve public control. Expensive databases may add value, but they will not define the boundary of a public right. Open the records without selling the key.","omitted":[],"refused":""}

Courts are steadily moving public records onto digital systems (dockets, filings, and orders), often with the advertised goal of making justice easier to observe. That goal is laudable. But access isn't truly public when ordinary people must buy an expensive private database subscription to find and read the work of a public court. Digitization should widen the courthouse door—it shouldn't replace the steps with a tollbooth.

Private vendors can offer useful tools (bulk search, alerts, analytics), and lawyers with demanding caseloads may reasonably pay for them. The problem begins when convenience becomes necessity. A vendor's polished index doesn't create the underlying record; courts, litigants, witnesses, jurors, and taxpayers create the system that produces it. If the only usable path runs through a commercial gatekeeper, public access depends on a company's prices, contracts, and product decisions. That arrangement also narrows who can notice patterns across cases (delay, unequal treatment, recurring errors) before those patterns become impossible to ignore. That isn't a public archive. It is a private map to public law.

Supporters of paid access often point to real costs (servers, redaction, security, staff). Those costs do not disappear because a record is viewed online, and privacy concerns deserve serious treatment. Yet charging high search or retrieval fees doesn't solve privacy. It merely sorts users by ability to pay. Wealthy firms can monitor cases at scale; reporters, researchers, small practices, families, and self-represented litigants can't. Paywalls also distort which disputes receive attention, because a story, study, or community inquiry may never begin when the first search demands money and the next courthouse demands another separate payment up front. A fee wall is a dragnet turned backward—it catches people by income rather than protecting sensitive information.

Consider the practical claim that records are “available” because anyone may request them (during office hours, under local procedures). Available how? If you had to visit several clerks, learn incompatible search rules, and pay repeatedly to trace one dispute, the legal right would remain while its practical value collapsed. Digital access can reproduce that maze (one court, one portal, one fee at a time) or replace it with a coherent public system. A right that works chiefly for specialists won't serve public oversight.

Courts also shouldn't outsource accountability for design choices. Search defaults, document labels, accessibility features (including screen-reader support), and correction processes shape what the public can discover. When those choices sit behind proprietary systems, agencies may blame vendors and vendors may point back to contracts—a loop with no clear owner. We believe courts must retain responsibility for the public interface, even when private companies supply software (hosting, indexing, or maintenance).

A sound policy can protect both access and privacy. Courts should publish records through searchable, accessible portals (with no charge for ordinary use), while applying clear redaction rules to sensitive fields (such as account numbers or minors' identifying details). Bulk access may require safeguards against abuse, but those safeguards should track conduct and risk; they should not make price the proxy for trust. Contractors can still compete to sell advanced services—public infrastructure often supports valuable private tools—without becoming the only practical route to the source material. Public access should be the floor on which better tools are built, not a stripped-down demo designed to push users toward a paid tier.

Lawmakers and court administrators should set a simple baseline: public records must be meaningfully reachable by the public. That means stable portals, understandable search, accessible formats, transparent redaction standards, and fees limited to exceptional costs rather than routine viewing. It also means preserving non-digital assistance (for people without reliable devices or connections). We urge legislatures and court systems to fund that baseline directly, audit vendors openly, and require contracts that preserve public control. Expensive databases may add value, but they will not define the boundary of a public right. Open the records without selling the key.
